analysis.one_liner: Removes the antitrust exemption that lets ocean shipping lines discuss and set freight rates together.
analysis.headline: Nine House members from both parties backed the bill, but it never received a committee markup or a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Ocean shipping companies are currently exempt from federal antitrust laws, meaning their agreements about freight rates are shielded from price-fixing suits. This short bill would repeal that exemption, exposing ocean carriers to the same antitrust enforcement as other industries. It was introduced during the supply-chain crisis, when shipping rates and carriers' profits hit record highs and those costs flowed into the prices consumers pay.
analysis.who_benefits: American importers, retailers, farmers, and ultimately consumers, who paid elevated freight costs embedded in the price of goods during the 2021-2022 shipping crunch. Repealing the exemption would let regulators and private lawsuits police carrier rate agreements the way antitrust law polices other industries.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals Section 40307 of title 46, U.S. Code, which exempts ocean common carriers from federal antitrust laws, and makes a conforming change to Section 40301(e).
The CRS summary states plainly that the bill removes the exemption from federal antitrust laws for ocean common carriers.

analysis.who_pays: Ocean shipping carriers, which would lose legal protection for rate discussions and face potential antitrust lawsuits and exposure. Some of that cost could be passed to shippers through higher risk premiums or changed service patterns.

drawbacks.text: Carrier alliances and rate 'discussion agreements' can let smaller lines pool vessels and offer regular service on routes that could not otherwise support them; removing the antitrust shield could disrupt those arrangements or make some routes less reliable.
Carriers facing antitrust exposure might charge shippers more to cover legal risk, and litigation costs would ultimately be passed through supply chains.
Repealing the exemption by itself does not address port congestion, equipment shortages, or other root causes of the 2021-2022 shipping crisis, so its practical effect on freight rates is uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit case was strongest in context: during 2021-2022, ocean carriers' rates and profits hit historic highs while the exemption shielded their rate coordination, and those freight costs fed into consumer prices. Repeal would have put shipping under the same antitrust rules as nearly every other industry. The honest counterargument is that the exemption also underwrites vessel-sharing alliances that keep service running on thin routes, and the bill does nothing to fix the physical supply-chain bottlenecks behind high rates. On balance a narrow, defensible bill whose cost falls mainly on a concentrated industry, but whose practical impact on consumer prices would have been gradual rather than immediate.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and two subcommittees, never received a markup or vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Costa (D-CA) introduced the bill on February 28, 2022, joined at introduction by Reps. Garamendi (D-CA), Smith of Nebraska (R), and Johnson of South Dakota (R).
Nine House members cosponsored the bill: 7 Democrats and 2 Republicans.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on the day of introduction.

It was later referred to the T&I Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation (March 1, 2022) and the Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law (November 1, 2022).
The action history shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ocean shipping carriers kept their antitrust exemption through the remainder of the record-profit pandemic shipping period, and shippers and consumers continued bearing the freight costs passed into prices. A separate, narrower ocean shipping reform bill became law in 2022, but it did not repeal the antitrust exemption.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ocean carriers, which kept the exemption

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — 7 Democrats and 2 Republicans cosponsored — and no recorded opposition vote; it simply never advanced.

industries.note: The bill would end these carriers' exemption from antitrust law, exposing their rate agreements to price-fixing suits, which matters because carriers earned record profits during the pandemic shipping surge while exemption shielded their coordination. Their interest in keeping the exemption ran against shippers and consumers, since higher freight costs flow into retail prices.

Importers and exporters bore record freight rates during 2021-2022; applying antitrust law to carrier rate agreements would give them a new check on coordinated pricing. Lower shipping costs would flow partly to consumers.
